notes:
These are verse-by-verse notes on Esther 10, with sources. I didn't find any verse where Protestant traditions really disagree, and I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Most of the material comes from older commentaries collected on biblehub.com and studylight.org, plus Enduring Word, The Gospel Coalition, Catholic and Wesleyan sources, and Bible Odyssey.

**Introduction to the chapter**

- Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic) treats the chapter as an epilogue. He uses it to look back over the whole book and what it teaches about God's providence, meaning God's hidden guidance of events. He walks us through how God's hand moved through entirely natural events—no miracles, no dramatic interventions—yet orchestrated countless details to preserve His people. He quotes Spurgeon (Baptist), who called Esther "a record of wonders without a miracle". He also teaches that God's will and human freedom both hold: Haman, the king, Mordecai and Esther each acted freely and were responsible, yet God worked through what they did. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-10/
- The Pulpit Commentary (Spanish edition on StudyLight) notes that a reader might have expected the book to end with the founding of Purim in chapter 9. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/tpc/esther-10.html
- The Cambridge Bible calls the link between this short chapter and the rest of the book "obscure." It may be a fragment of another work, or simply a postscript meant to show the king's power and so add to Mordecai's glory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-1.htm

**v. 1: The king's tribute**

- **Why the tax?** Ellicott says the failed invasion of Greece had drained the empire, so new tribute was needed to refill the treasury. A war was also still going on along the coast of Asia Minor. https://biblehub.com/esther/10-1.htm
- Gill offers the same Greek-war explanation. He also mentions another view: the king was bringing back taxes he had cancelled when he married Esther (2:18). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/esther-10.html
- The Gospel Coalition commentary (David Firth) reads the verse as a sign that ordinary life has resumed after Haman's chaos. The tax may have been forced labour, perhaps to pay for the costs Haman's decree caused. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/esther/
- **The Hebrew word.** The Cambridge Bible says that everywhere else in the Hebrew Bible this word means a body of forced labourers, so it should read "imposed forced labour." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-1.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch say the word for "service" stands for tribute here. Provinces mostly paid in produce, so their farm labour was a kind of service to the king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-1.htm
- The NET Bible translates it as "imposed forced labor". https://biblehub.com/esther/10-1.htm
- **"Islands / farthest shores."** Ellicott says Cyprus was the main island Persia still held. The Aegean islands had broken free, so the old title may simply have been kept, the way royal titles sometimes outlast lost lands. https://biblehub.com/esther/10-1.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the Hebrew phrase includes coastal strips. Xerxes may have assessed tax on the Aegean islands even if he couldn't collect it. It adds that Darius was the first to set the tribute, but later kings who rearranged it could also be said to "lay a tribute." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-10.html
- Barnes suggests Cyprus, Aradus and the island of Tyre, among others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-1.htm
- **Mordecai's part.** The Pulpit Homiletics section (W. Dinwiddie) thinks the tax was probably a major reform. It credits the reform to Mordecai as an example of his wisdom, and draws lessons about fair taxation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-10.html
- The Bridgeway Bible Commentary reads it differently: under Mordecai, non-Jewish peoples were made to pay more, which eased the burden on the Jews. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/10-2.html
- **Application.** Bible Hub's study notes say God's providence carries on through ordinary government after the dramatic rescue. https://biblehub.com/esther/10-1.htm

**v. 2: The royal chronicles**

- **The king's power and Mordecai's.** Benson says the king's great deeds should be credited largely to Mordecai's management. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-2.htm
- Matthew Henry says the king never did such mighty things as when Mordecai was his right hand. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/10-2.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says it is especially honourable that even the records of pagan kings had to remember Mordecai. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/esther-10.html
- **What the chronicles were.** Keil and Delitzsch think the author used these chronicles as a source. Ending with a reference to them follows the same pattern as Kings and Chronicles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-2.htm
- The Cambridge Bible says the wording may be copied from formulas like 1 Kings 14:19. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-2.htm
- Constable says the appeal to the chronicles claims the events really happened. The documents are lost, and they may have been either Persian or Jewish archives. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/10-2.html
- **Why Media comes before Persia.** Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary say the Median kingdom came first in time, so its history came first in the book. The Pulpit Commentary adds that we don't know the deeds referred to; Xerxes' later energy seems to have gone mainly into grand buildings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-2.htm
- **Application.** Matthew Henry notes that the Persian chronicles are long lost while Scripture lasts. In his view the Holy Spirit counts the affairs of God's despised worshippers as more important than any king's exploits. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-2.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary sees God's special care for His word in the fact that Esther survived while the chronicles perished. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/esther-10.html

**v. 3: Mordecai's greatness**

- **"Second to the king."** Gill calls him the second man in the kingdom and chief minister. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-3.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary compares Joseph (Genesis 41:40) and Daniel. It adds that non-biblical history neither confirms nor contradicts Mordecai's rank. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-3.htm
- Ellicott dates the high point of Mordecai's power to about 470 BC. We don't know how long it lasted; near the end of Xerxes' reign his favourite was Artabanus, who murdered him in 464 BC. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-3.htm
- **"Highly favoured by his kinsmen."** Benson, Poole and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) all say his people didn't envy him but thanked God for him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-3.htm
- Gill reads "many" as most rather than all, because a deserving man will always have some critics. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-3.htm
- **"Seeking the good of his people."** Benson stresses that Mordecai worked for his people's welfare, not his own fortune. Henry adds that he didn't disown his people and no doubt kept the true faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-3.htm
- **"Speaking peace to all his countrymen."** Gill gives two possible meanings: speaking kindly to the Jews, or speaking up for them before the king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-3.htm
- Benson thinks "all" means he took no sides between factions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-3.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary takes it to mean securing their peace and safety for as long as he ruled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-3.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch say Mordecai brought about his people's good by both word and deed. They tie this to Psalm 34. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-2.htm
- Coffman suggests Mordecai was probably a eunuch, so "his seed" means Israel as a whole. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/10-2.html
- **Application.** The Geneva Study Bible draws three marks of a good ruler from the verse: the people's favour, working for their wealth, and gentleness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-3.htm
- JFB sees God's providence in Mordecai's rise, working through ordinary events as with Joseph. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/10-3.htm
- Guzik ends by pointing to Jesus as the believer's advocate "near the throne." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-10/
- Firth (TGC) notes the irony: in an empire that tried to destroy the Jews, a Jew is now second only to the king. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/esther/
- **Was there a real Mordecai?** A Bible Hub article admits no Persian record clearly names him. It mentions inconclusive references to a "Marduka" in tablets and argues the account is still plausible. https://biblehub.com/q/is_there_persian_proof_of_mordecai's_rank.htm

**Differences between Protestant traditions**

- I found no real disagreement on these verses. Reformed (Geneva, Henry, Poole), Baptist (Gill, Spurgeon), Methodist (Benson, Clarke) and Pentecostal (Guzik) writers all stress providence and Mordecai as a model of leadership. I didn't read Wesley's own notes, and found nothing Lutheran or Anglican-specific.

**Other views**

- **After v. 3, Catholic and Orthodox Bibles keep going.** Clarke notes that the Hebrew text ends at v. 3. The Vulgate and Greek add ten more verses here, plus six more chapters, for sixteen in all. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/esther-10.html
- The Catholic Encyclopedia counts "the supplement to Esther, from x, 4, to the end" as deuterocanonical, meaning part of the Catholic canon (Protestants call these books the Apocrypha). It says the additions were probably written first in Hebrew. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/03267a.htm
- In the Catholic Public Domain Version, v. 3 runs straight into Mordecai saying these things were done by God, recalling a dream he had about them. https://biblehub.com/parallel/esther/10-3.htm
- The Wesley Center calls this section Addition F, the interpretation of Mordecai's dream. The additions are in Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments and among the Protestant Apocrypha. They probably date from the 2nd or 1st century BC and add many references to God. https://wesley.nnu.edu/sermons-essays-books/noncanonical-literature/noncanonical-literature-ot-apocrypha/additions-to-esther/
- Catholic Answers says the liturgy prefers the Greek passages because they make explicit what the Hebrew writer only hints at. It also says the author had access to Persian chronicles, citing 10:2. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/judith-and-esther
- **Modern scholarship.** Bible Odyssey notes that both the Greek and Hebrew versions had authority in the ancient world. It says interpreters from the rabbis of antiquity to Martin Luther and beyond struggled with the book's status as Scripture. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/esther/
- **Protestant view of the additions.** Don Stewart (Blue Letter Bible) says the additions have no historical basis. In the dream, one dragon stands for Haman and the other for Mordecai. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/books-missing-from-old-testament/question2-contents-apocrypha.cfm

**Gaps:** Precept Austin's Esther 10 notes were cut off before I could read them. I didn't see NET Bible study notes beyond its translation, or anything on oca.org.
